analysis.summary:
Read-only analysis by Claude (automated agent) of the retained evidence for the failed 30 September CODEX-S25-MATRIX-01 attempt (candidate 68ba0622). I changed no repository files. Scratch scripts are in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Spheres/e3d5a311-d2fe-504d-bb9f-1264447cf21c/scratchpad/s25-crash-analysis/ (timeline.py, state.py). Nothing here is a qualification, acceptance or root-cause claim.

Main findings:
(1) Between 17:43:07 and 23:29:02 UTC exactly four native processes ran: japan-7, japan-42, india-1990 and india-7. Japan/7 and India/7 had access violations in ntdll 16.76 s apart, at different simulated dates (2031-01 and 2024-12). If their fault times were independent, a gap that small has roughly a 0.16% chance. This points to an event on the machine at about 23:28, not a deterministic simulation-date defect.
(2) The exit code 1 for Japan/42 and India/1990 matches CPython's Popen.kill() on Windows, which calls TerminateProcess(handle, 1). The runner calls kill() after a retention failure, and the test binary has no reachable exit(1). The four partial cells all show the same artifacts: archive raw_removed false, a transfer.json present, no verdict.json. That is the runner's code path when its journal write fails right after the crash.
(3) Every long-lived handle on D: had failed by 23:29–23:30: the runner journal, the launcher stdout/stderr and the verifier events log. New handles on D: were working at the same time. D: is recorded as the external USB drive. Separately, a political build on D: that same evening failed with "device not ready" while all four workers were still running.
(4) At 23:28, the leader-art release compile was running on the same machine. Codex's notes from that evening treat memory as a constraint on how many builds could run at once. A baseline measured later (01 Oct 03:26 UTC), with the matrix not running, had only 8.75 GB of commit headroom.
(5) The matrix workers' own state size at the crash was lower than during wave 1, which finished cleanly.
(6) The exception signature does not fit the standard mechanism of any hypothesis. A Rust heap-exhaustion failure would show 0xc0000409 plus a stderr message. A failed page-in from the D:-hosted image would show 0xc0000006. Only a dump can settle this.
(7) The Linux rerun the parent believes is running is not running. It exited 101 at 2026-10-04T01:14:01Z because run.sh pre-creates SPHERES_S25_OUT, and the test requires a new directory.

hypotheses.claim: The machine ran out of commit or memory at about 23:28 UTC. The likely drivers are the four long-lived matrix workers, which make large transient monthly allocations (a whole-world serde_json::Value DOM, multiple world copies and ~130–180 MB strings), plus concurrent release-mode cargo compiles/tests and desktop apps. The matrix's own state did not grow with simulated date. Under this pressure, two workers faulted inside ntdll.
supporting_evidence: Two independent processes at different simulated dates (2031-01 and 2024-12) faulted 16.76 s apart. The chance of that with independent timing is about 0.16%, which points to a shared environmental trigger.

The leader-art release compile of spheres-web (CARGO_BUILD_JOBS=1) ran from 23:19:04 to about 23:31:21, covering both faults. A political release-build effort was also active 22:52–23:36 (attempt-02/results.json, console.log; GitHub commit times).

Memory was treated as a constraint that evening: workspace-01 was stopped at 23:52 'to resume … with two build jobs after memory became available'. A 2-job compile at 23:13–23:17 exited 101 during compilation with no diagnostic.
With the matrix not running, baseline commit was 41.42 of 50.18 GB, leaving only 8.75 GB of headroom (diagnostic preflight.json, 1 Oct 03:26).

Per-worker scale: early-1990 workers on ae8084e8 already peaked at 0.79–0.83 GiB pagefile usage. A two-world 1994 process peaked at 1.06 GB. The 68ba0622 code path adds a Value DOM and a third decoded world at monthly saves, so four workers could plausibly need several GB at once.
Japan/42 and India/1990 survived for 47+ s after the faults. That fits transient pressure that hits only processes allocating at that moment.
contrary_evidence: Rust's heap-exhaustion path prints 'memory allocation of N bytes failed' to stderr and fails fast with 0xc0000409. The observed code is 0xc0000005 in ntdll and stderr.log is empty in both crashed cells.
A failure to commit a new stack page normally surfaces as STATUS_STACK_OVERFLOW (0xc00000fd), not 0xc0000005.

Estimated from canonical bytes, the matrix's own state load at the crash (~541 MB) was below wave 1's maximum (~709 MB), and wave 1 finished. Extra pressure would have to come from outside the matrix, and wave 1's external load is unknown.
No commit, memory or Resource-Exhaustion-Detector observation exists for 23:28. The 8.75 GB headroom was measured about 4 h later under different load.
The isolated single-process Japan/7 diagnostic ran 12 h with no resource halt, but that was a different load and it is unknown whether it reached January 2031.
hypotheses.linux_test: Relaunch the 68ba0622 Japan/7 rerun with SPHERES_S25_OUT set to a directory that does not exist yet (remove 'mkdir -p $D/native' from run.sh). Every 30 s, read VmRSS, VmHWM, RssAnon and VmData from /proc/PID/status plus the last end_native_date in progress.jsonl, then run 'echo 5 > /proc/PID/clear_refs' to reset VmHWM. Each row then holds that window's peak; plain 30-s VmRSS samples miss the monthly transients. Run under /usr/bin/time -v as well. If per-process window peaks are ≥2 GB, then 4 × peak plus a 1–3 GB compile reaches the ~8.75 GB Windows headroom, and H1 is arithmetically plausible. If the peaks stay ≲0.5 GB, H1 needs implausibly large external load. Caveat: Linux glibc RSS is not Windows commit. Optionally run a short second job under 'ulimit -v' just below the observed VmPeak to capture this binary's exhaustion signature (expected: the Rust allocation-failure message and SIGABRT). That shows plain heap exhaustion is loud, which bears on the empty-stderr contrary point.

hypotheses.claim: A transient failure of the external-USB D: volume ('device not ready') invalidated every long-lived handle on D:. That explains the lost journal writes and, through the runner's own exception path, the exit-1 kills, the launcher exit 120 and the verifier PermissionError. Because D: also backs the mapped 353 MB test executable, the same event may have contributed to the native faults, possibly together with H1 memory pressure forcing image pages to be re-read.
supporting_evidence: Three separate long-lived D: write handles had all failed by 23:29–23:30: the runner journal (open since 09:03), the launcher stdout/stderr (0 bytes, exit 120) and the verifier events.jsonl (open since 10:02). New handles on D: worked at the same time: transfer.json, copied files, the verifier result.json, full-exit.json and binary rehashes.

The verifier's 'PermissionError: [Errno 13]' has no filename or WinError, which fits a write, flush or fsync on an already-open descriptor. To my knowledge (general Windows/CRT knowledge, not from the repo), the MS CRT maps Win32 errors 5 and 19–36, including ERROR_NOT_READY (21), to EACCES.
On the same evening a D: build failed with 'PowerShell log write: device not ready' while all four matrix workers were running (political-repairs-20260930/storage-preflight.json).
A D: build failed during compilation with exit 101 and no diagnostic between 23:13:58 and 23:17:53 (leader-art attempt-01).
D: is documented as the external USB drive, and the executable, journal and logs all lived on it.
contrary_evidence: A failed page-in from a file-backed image normally raises STATUS_IN_PAGE_ERROR (0xc0000006), usually in the exe or CRT. WER records 0xc0000005 in ntdll.
The D: failure time is not recorded. If it was about 23:14–23:18, it was 10+ minutes before the faults.
D: was readable again by 23:29:02, when the binary_after rehash matched the pin, and later builds targeting D: succeeded from 23:19.
The journal-break time is bounded only to 17:43–23:29 and the verifier's to 10:02–23:30, so a common timing with the faults is not shown.
NTFS compression applied only to the C: scratch. The native monthly writes there succeeded for 405–492 reloads per cell, and a write error would have been recorded as a Rust Err with exit 101.

One feasible container check: run the frozen local-matrix-20260930/stability_matrix.py on Linux with a fake native binary (a script that sleeps, or exits with a signal) and a monkeypatched journal whose write or flush raises PermissionError(13) after N events. Confirm it reproduces the exact retained pattern: archive record with raw_removed false and no .bak archive, transfer.json present, no verdict.json, the surviving children killed by Popen.kill, and no result.json. That would attribute the exit-1 codes to the runner's own kill path. The decisive checks for the D: event are on Windows (see open questions).

hypotheses.claim: A latent heap-corruption or memory-safety fault, in std, serde/serde_json, the windows-gnu toolchain or an injected third-party DLL, produced access violations inside ntdll heap routines.
supporting_evidence: Access violations inside ntdll at different offsets (0x166167 and 0x10579) with no Rust message are a classic heap-corruption signature.
Both crashed cells are seed 7, though France/7 passed.
contrary_evidence: spheres-sim/src and spheres-web/src contain no unsafe code at 68ba0622, and dependencies are limited to serde/serde_json (git grep).
The same binary passed four full-horizon cells under the same 4-way concurrency.
A code-intrinsic corruption does not explain two separate processes faulting 16.76 s apart.
The isolated Japan/7 diagnostic ran 12 h without a captured native failure, though it may not have reached January 2031 and probably ran with the debug heap.
hypotheses.linux_test: In the corrected Japan/7 rerun (or a parallel India/7 rerun), set GLIBC_TUNABLES=glibc.malloc.check=3:glibc.malloc.perturb=165. That is low-overhead heap-misuse detection and freed-memory poisoning that makes use-after-free more likely to crash. A clean pass through the crash windows weakens H6 for platform-independent code. ASan/Miri over the full horizon is not practical in this container. A one-month ASan replay from the retained 2031-01-01 monthly.json would be feasible if that external D: file were made available.

hypotheses.claim: A deterministic simulation or code defect triggers at a specific simulated state: Japan/7 during January 2031 and India/7 during December 2024.
supporting_evidence: Each fault happened at a specific simulated window after a known checkpoint (Japan/7 fnv a1bd0d0f4f98ac5f at 2031-01-01; India/7 6889dd30b08580b8 at 2024-12-01).
The cells that faulted were not the ones that were killed, which fits state-specific triggers.
contrary_evidence: The two faults are 16.76 s apart in wall time at unrelated simulated dates. A deterministic state trigger would not line up in wall time (chance about 0.16%).
All retained comparisons matched up to the last checkpoint, and the reports record no Rust failure.
An access violation in safe Rust with no unsafe project code is not the expected signature of a logic defect, which would surface as an Err, a panic (exit 101) or a stack overflow.
hypotheses.linux_test: In the corrected single-process 68ba0622 Japan/7 rerun, compare every comparison row (date, canonical_bytes, canonical_fnv64, history_rows, log_rows) with the 1,027 retained Windows rows through 2031-01-01. An exact match proves the same trajectory across platforms. If it then passes the 2031-02-01 checkpoint and the full horizon without failure, a platform-independent state-triggered defect at that point is refuted. Repeat for India/7 against its 872 rows through 2024-12-01 and past 2025-01-01. If fingerprints diverge (for example from libm differences), the test only weakly addresses H2. At Windows pace, Japan/7 needs about 7 h to reach 2031.

hypotheses.claim: Stack exhaustion on the libtest test thread (default 2 MiB) during deep recursive serialization or validation.
supporting_evidence: The fault is inside a system DLL with no Rust panic recorded.
Serde serialization and the CheckedJson validation walk are recursive.
contrary_evidence: Stack overflow on Windows is 0xc00000fd, and Rust's handler prints 'thread … has overflowed its stack' to stderr. The observed code is 0xc0000005 and stderr is empty.

Recursion depth is set by the state shape, which would make the failure deterministic and not tied to wall-clock timing. The state was smaller at the crash than at the 2010 peak, which every cell survived.
serde_json's default 128-level recursion limit was satisfied by 405–492 successful monthly decodes per cell.
hypotheses.linux_test: Check the corrected rerun's stderr for Rust's overflow message. Then run a second Linux job with RUST_MIN_STACK=524288 (one quarter of the default) at least through the 2008–2012 peak-state compares. Passing means at least 4× stack margin at peak state and refutes H3.

hypotheses.claim: A hardware fault (RAM or CPU) or a third-party injected or system component hit two processes at once.
supporting_evidence: The near-simultaneous faults point to an event outside the program.
Different ntdll offsets suggest unrelated code paths.
contrary_evidence: Random hardware errors rarely hit two processes within 17 s.
The machine completed four full cells the same day.
No WHEA, security-software or injected-module evidence was collected.
hypotheses.linux_test: Linux cannot discriminate this, since it runs on different hardware. A clean Linux pass is merely consistent. Needs Windows WHEA-Logger and security-product logs, and a dump module list.

verdicts.reasoning:
Reviewer: Claude, an automated agent. This is not a human or Codex review. Verdict: the evidence does not disprove H1, but it does not support it either. Under the default rule for unsupported hypotheses, H1 is refuted, and its medium confidence is overstated.

No commit or memory reading exists for 23:28. The only fault signature is 0xc0000005 in ntdll with an empty stderr.log, and that does not match Rust's out-of-memory path. Most of the cited numbers do check out. They show a busy machine, but they say nothing about what caused the crash.

What I confirmed against the files:
- **Fault times:** the Event 1000 times in windows-crashes.json are 23:28:41.129Z and 23:28:57.885Z, which is 16.76 s apart. The WER EventTime values give 17.09 s.
